request.user:
[2019 fall ms applied — problem 5]

July temperatures (°F) in New Brunswick and Piscataway on the same randomly chosen date in each of 7 years; measures in different years independent, but the two cities on the same day are not. (A) Give point estimates of each city's mean July temperature and the standard errors. (B) Give a 95% prediction interval for next year's New Brunswick temperature. (C) Test whether the two cities' mean July temperatures are equal at level 0.05.

response.text:
The numerical data table is not included in the prompt, so numerical estimates and the final reject/fail-to-reject decision cannot be computed. But the correct analysis is as follows.

Let

\[
X_i=\text{New Brunswick temperature in year }i,\qquad
Y_i=\text{Piscataway temperature in year }i,
\]

for \(i=1,\dots,7\). The pairs \((X_i,Y_i)\) are independent across years, but \(X_i\) and \(Y_i\) within the same year/date may be correlated.

Let

\[
\bar X=\frac1{7}\sum_{i=1}^7 X_i,\qquad 
\bar Y=\frac1{7}\sum_{i=1}^7 Y_i,
\]

and

\[
s_X^2=\frac1{6}\sum_{i=1}^7 (X_i-\bar X)^2,\qquad
s_Y^2=\frac1{6}\sum_{i=1}^7 (Y_i-\bar Y)^2.
\]

---

## (A) Point estimates and standard errors

The point estimates of the two city mean July temperatures are

\[
\widehat{\mu}_X=\bar X,\qquad \widehat{\mu}_Y=\bar Y.
\]

The estimated standard errors are

\[
\operatorname{SE}(\bar X)=\frac{s_X}{\sqrt{7}},
\qquad
\operatorname{SE}(\bar Y)=\frac{s_Y}{\sqrt{7}}.
\]

The within-year dependence does not affect these marginal standard errors, because the observations are independent across years for each city.

---

## (B) 95% prediction interval for next year's New Brunswick temperature

Assuming the New Brunswick temperatures are approximately normally distributed, a 95% prediction interval for a single future New Brunswick temperature \(X_{\text{new}}\) is

\[
\bar X \pm t_{0.975,6}\, s_X\sqrt{1+\frac1{7}}.
\]

Since

\[
t_{0.975,6}\approx 2.447,
\]

the interval is

\[
\boxed{
\bar X \pm 2.447\, s_X\sqrt{\frac{8}{7}}
}.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\boxed{
\left(
\bar X-2.447\, s_X\sqrt{\frac87},
\;
\bar X+2.447\, s_X\sqrt{\frac87}
\right)
}.
\]

---

## (C) Test whether the two cities have equal mean July temperatures

Because the two temperatures are measured on the same date in the same year, this is a paired-sample problem, not an independent two-sample problem.

Define the paired differences

\[
D_i=X_i-Y_i,\qquad i=1,\dots,7.
\]

We test

\[
H_0:\mu_D=0
\]

against the two-sided alternative

\[
H_a:\mu_D\neq 0.
\]

Let

\[
\bar D=\frac1{7}\sum_{i=1}^7 D_i
\]

and

\[
s_D^2=\frac1{6}\sum_{i=1}^7 (D_i-\bar D)^2.
\]

The paired \(t\)-statistic is

\[
T=\frac{\bar D}{s_D/\sqrt{7}}.
\]

Under \(H_0\), assuming approximate normality of the paired differences,

\[
T\sim t_6.
\]

At level \(\alpha=0.05\), the two-sided rejection rule is

\[
|T|>t_{0.975,6}=2.447.
\]

So the test is:

\[
\boxed{
\text{Reject }H_0 \text{ if }
\left|\frac{\bar D}{s_D/\sqrt{7}}\right|>2.447.
}
\]

Equivalently, compute the \(p\)-value

\[
p=2P\left(t_6>|T|\right),
\]

and reject \(H_0\) if \(p<0.05\).

Without the actual temperature data, the numerical test statistic and conclusion cannot be determined.
